speaker.role: organizational behavior lecturer explaining workplace mentorship program outcomes

academicTalks.transcript: Today I want to talk about how companies structure mentorship programs, and what actually predicts whether they work. Most programs pair a newer employee with someone more senior, but the pairing method matters a lot. Programs that let employees choose their own mentor, rather than being assigned one at random, tend to show better outcomes. In one study following several companies over three years, researchers tracked promotion rates among employees who had a mentor versus those who didn't. Employees with a self-selected mentor were promoted at nearly twice the rate of those without any mentor at all, while randomly assigned pairs showed only a modest improvement. Retention told a similar story. Mentees who chose their own mentor stayed at the company noticeably longer than mentees in randomly assigned pairs, who left at rates close to employees with no mentor. The researchers suggest that choice itself builds trust between mentor and mentee, which makes the relationship more likely to lead to real guidance rather than a check-the-box meeting once a month.

questions.stem: What is the talk mainly about?

options.text: How companies should redesign their onboarding manuals for new hires.
The origins and historical spread of corporate mentorship programs.
How mentor-pairing methods shape promotion and retention.
Why mentorship programs should be phased out at most companies.

questions.explanationZh: 整篇談的是師徒配對方式如何影響升遷與留任率，對應開頭「what actually predicts whether they work」；其餘選項提到新人手冊設計、停止提供師徒制、歷史沿革，原文皆未提及。

questions.stem: According to the talk, how did self-selected mentor pairs compare to employees with no mentor?

options.text: Promotion data wasn't collected for that group.
They were promoted at nearly twice the rate.
They were promoted slightly less often.
They were promoted at exactly the same rate.

questions.explanationZh: 講者提到自選導師的員工「promoted at nearly twice the rate of those without any mentor」；其餘選項提到升遷率相同、略低、未收集資料，原文皆未提及。

speaker.role: public administration lecturer explaining a neighborhood watch program's effect on reported incidents

academicTalks.transcript: Let's look at what happens when a city rolls out a neighborhood watch program block by block, rather than all at once. One city government phased in volunteer patrols over eighteen months, starting with a handful of neighborhoods and expanding gradually based on volunteer interest. This staggered rollout let researchers compare reported incident rates in blocks that already had a watch program against blocks still waiting for one. Blocks with an active program saw reported minor incidents, things like vandalism and package theft, drop by close to a third within six months. Interestingly, reports of more serious crimes didn't change much either way — the effect showed up almost entirely in smaller, opportunistic offenses. Researchers also mapped volunteer patrol coverage against incident locations and found that blocks with patrols scheduled during evening hours saw the steepest drop, since that's when opportunistic incidents were most common. The takeaway wasn't that watch programs eliminate crime, but that visible, well-timed volunteer presence changes the calculation for someone considering a low-risk, opportunistic act.

questions.stem: What is the main finding discussed in the talk?

options.text: A staggered rollout reduced minor incident reports in blocks with active patrols.
Neighborhood watch programs showed no measurable effect on overall local crime rates.
Volunteer interest in the watch program declined steadily over the eighteen months.
Serious crimes fell sharply in nearly every block once patrols began operating.

questions.explanationZh: 整段核心是分階段推動守望相助後，已實施街區的輕微案件明顯下降，對應「reported minor incidents... drop by close to a third」；其餘選項提到完全無效、重大犯罪大幅下降、志工興趣下降，原文皆未提及或與內容相反。

questions.stem: According to the talk, what happened to reports of serious crimes?

options.text: They were not tracked in the study.
They increased in blocks with patrols.
They didn't change much either way.
They dropped by a third, same as minor incidents.

questions.explanationZh: 講者明確說「reports of more serious crimes didn't change much either way」；其餘選項提到增加、與輕微案件一樣下降三分之一、未被追蹤，原文皆未提及。

questions.stem: Which blocks saw the steepest drop in incidents?

Those with patrols scheduled during evening hours.
Those that started the program first.
Those closest to the police station.

Volunteer patrols should replace police patrols entirely.

speaker.role: computer science lecturer explaining how streaming software throttles video quality on slow connections

academicTalks.transcript: When you're streaming video on a slow connection, you've probably noticed the picture gets blurrier instead of just freezing. That's adaptive streaming at work. The software constantly estimates your connection speed, usually by measuring how long recent chunks of video took to download, and checks that estimate every few seconds. If the estimate drops below what the current video quality needs, the player switches to a lower-resolution version of the same content for the next chunk, rather than waiting and risking a stall. One study comparing streaming platforms found that checking the connection speed too often, say, every second, actually made buffering worse, because the player kept switching quality levels back and forth instead of settling on a stable one. Platforms that checked every five to ten seconds instead saw noticeably less buffering overall, since the player had time to confirm a speed estimate before acting on it. The lesson researchers drew was that responsiveness has a sweet spot — react too slowly and viewers stall, react too quickly and the constant quality switching becomes its own kind of disruption.

questions.stem: What does adaptive streaming software do when it detects a slower connection?

options.text: It downloads the whole video before resuming playback.
It pauses playback completely until the connection fully recovers to normal speed.
It switches to a lower-quality version for the next chunk.
It shortens the video by trimming out some content.

questions.explanationZh: 講者說明連線變慢時，播放器會「switches to a lower-resolution version...for the next chunk, rather than waiting and risking a stall」，即切換低畫質而非暫停、整支下載完才播，也不是縮短影片長度。

questions.stem: According to the study mentioned, what happened when platforms checked connection speed every second?

options.text: The study found no measurable difference at all.
Buffering got worse due to constant quality switching.
Video resolution stayed fixed the whole time.
Buffering disappeared almost entirely.

questions.explanationZh: 講者提到每秒檢查一次反而「made buffering worse, because the player kept switching quality levels back and forth」；其餘選項提到緩衝幾乎消失、畫質全程不變、無明顯差異，原文皆未提及。

questions.stem: What checking interval performed better, according to the talk?

options.text: Every five to ten seconds.
Only once per video session.
Every thirty seconds or more.
Every second, matched exactly to playback.

questions.explanationZh: 講者指出每五到十秒檢查一次的平台「saw noticeably less buffering overall」；其餘選項提到三十秒以上、整段影片只檢查一次、每秒檢查，原文皆未提及或與結論相反。

questions.stem: What is the speaker's overall conclusion about checking frequency?

options.text: Checking frequency should always be increased as much as technically possible for best results.
There is a sweet spot between responsiveness and stability.
Checking frequency has no real effect on buffering.
Slower checking always produces the best results.

questions.explanationZh: 講者結論「responsiveness has a sweet spot — react too slowly and viewers stall, react too quickly and...disruption」，說明過快過慢皆有問題，並非愈快愈好、毫無影響或愈慢愈好。

speaker.role: transportation planning lecturer explaining how dynamic ticket pricing affects train seat occupancy

academicTalks.transcript: Train operators have started using dynamic pricing, where ticket prices shift based on expected demand, much like airlines have done for years. I want to walk through what happened when one regional rail line switched from flat fares to a dynamic model. Before the change, seat occupancy during peak morning hours regularly exceeded ninety percent, while midday trains often ran less than half full. After switching to dynamic pricing, peak fares rose during the busiest hour, while midday and early-evening fares dropped noticeably to attract riders who had flexibility in their schedule. Within four months, midday occupancy climbed from under fifty percent to around seventy percent, as some commuters shifted their trips slightly to take advantage of the lower fares. Peak occupancy actually eased slightly too, since a portion of riders who could adjust their schedule chose to avoid the higher peak price. The operator didn't add a single additional train to the schedule — the shift in when people rode accounted for the entire change in occupancy patterns across the day.

questions.explanationZh: 整段講的是動態票價如何改變某鐵路的座位使用率分布，對應「switched from flat fares to a dynamic model」及後續占座率變化；其餘選項提到取消尖峰班次、航空公司定價、平價制歷史，原文皆未提及。

questions.explanationZh: 講者明確說「midday occupancy climbed from under fifty percent to around seventy percent」；其餘選項提到繼續下降、維持不變、達到尖峰時段的九成以上，原文皆未提及。

questions.explanationZh: 講者說「riders who could adjust their schedule chose to avoid the higher peak price」，因此有彈性的乘客改到離峰時段；其餘選項提到取消尖峰班次、座位限制、需預先訂位，原文皆未提及。

questions.stem: What does the speaker note about the number of trains during this change?

questions.explanationZh: 講者強調「The operator didn't add a single additional train to the schedule」，說明占座率變化純粹來自乘車時間的改變；其餘選項提到增加班次一倍、移除尖峰班次、未提及班次數，原文皆與此矛盾或不符。
